design_detail: Narrative review of human cannabinoid pharmacokinetics by a single author from the Intramural Research Program of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse: absorption by route (smoked, oral, oromucosal, rectal, transdermal, intravenous), distribution, metabolism and elimination of THC, 11-OH-THC, THC-COOH and CBD, and the interpretation of cannabinoid concentrations in plasma, urine, oral fluid, sweat and hair. No search strategy or selection criteria; 189 references; six figures, all from the author's own studies. Read as the PMC author manuscript of the published article (Chem Biodivers 2007;4(8):1770–1804), which has no abstract.
can_establish: What controlled-administration studies up to about 2006 had shown, as summarised by a leading laboratory, about how the route changes the speed, height and duration of THC exposure (peaks within minutes after smoking; slower, lower, later and more variable peaks after oral intake, with relatively more 11-OH-THC and longer effects), about THC storage in fat and slow terminal elimination with frequent use, and about detection windows in blood, urine, oral fluid and hair.
cannot_establish: Whether these figures describe current products and patterns of use (the data come mostly from single smoked doses of cigarettes with 1.75% to 3.55% THC in small groups, with participants' sex given for only a few studies (mostly men where given), with little on daily use, high-THC edibles, vaporizers or concentrates), any health effect of cannabis, or impairment at a given blood concentration (the review itself notes that concentrations and effects diverge); and, with no systematic search or appraisal, whether the cited evidence is complete.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The human data summarised come mostly from small controlled-administration studies, for example 6 participants (sex not stated) smoking cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC with continuous blood sampling (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992), 6 volunteers taking THC in hemp oil or dronabinol for 5 days (Gustafson et al. 2003; Goodwin et al. 2006), 8 men given intravenous THC (Kelly & Jones 1992), 17 volunteers given a dronabinol capsule (Kim & Yoon 1996) and 38 men in a hair study (Huestis et al. 2007).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the author.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the author's own. All six figures and much of the quantitative human material (smoked and oral plasma kinetics, urinary excretion and detection times, time-of-use prediction models, creatinine ratios, oral fluid, hair) come from the author's laboratory, including conference presentations and unpublished observations. Distribution and metabolism rest partly on animal studies (rats, mice, guinea pigs, rabbits, dogs, pigs, monkeys).

exposure.measurement: Controlled administration in the cited human studies: smoked cigarettes of stated THC content, oral THC (dronabinol capsules, hemp oil, a chocolate cookie, capsules of THC in sesame oil), oromucosal extracts, suppositories, a transdermal patch and intravenous THC; analytes measured by GC/MS or GC/MS/MS, while early studies used radiolabels, which the author says overestimated THC.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported, not guidance: smoked cigarettes of 1% to 3.55% THC (about 16 to 34 mg per cigarette in the author's studies); oral THC as single doses of 10 to 20 mg, or 0.39 to 14.8 mg a day for 5 days; intravenous THC 2.5 to 5 mg. Daily or long-term use is represented by a few studies (Peat 1989; Johansson et al. 1988, 1989; Lafolie et al. 1991; Fraser & Worth 2002 to 2004). Vaporization is mentioned in one sentence without data; there are no data on concentrates or high-dose edibles.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; the controlled studies gave THC or cannabis alone, and tobacco or alcohol co-use is not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable in the usual sense; detection windows depend on prior use (for example residual plasma THC below 2 ng/ml about 12 hours after smoking in people with frequent use, and urine positive for up to 67 days in one person, and cannabinoids detectable in urine for 93 days in another, with heavy long-term use).

comparison.controls: Within-study comparisons of routes, doses and frequent against occasional use in the cited studies; no control group in the review's sense.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (pharmacokinetic review). Sex differences get one sentence (no significant differences in metabolism between men and women, citing Wall et al. 1983); where the review gives participants' sex, they were mostly men (eight men given intravenous THC, 20 male volunteers, 38 men in the hair study; women and men in Wall et al.), and the 6-person smoking studies are given without sex.

outcomes.instruments: Concentrations of THC, 11-OH-THC, THC-COOH (free and glucuronide) and CBD in plasma, whole blood, urine, oral fluid, sweat, hair and post-mortem tissue, by GC/MS, GC/MS/MS, LC/MS/MS, immunoassay or radioimmunoassay; pharmacokinetic parameters (peak, time to peak, bioavailability, volume of distribution, clearance, half-lives); detection times at stated cut-offs.
outcomes.validity_norms: The author discusses analytical limits: very low concentrations, adsorption of cannabinoids to containers and collection devices, hydrolysis methods that miss glucuronide conjugates, short sampling windows that underestimate half-lives, and radiolabel methods that overestimate THC.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable (no harm outcome); impairment is discussed only through suggested blood concentrations.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, each figure with its primary source (see key findings). Smoked THC: bioavailability 2% to 56% (Agurell & Leander 1971; Ohlsson et al. 1982, 1985; Agurell et al. 1986) or about 8% to 24% (Ohlsson et al. 1980; Perez-Reyes et al. 1981; Lindgren et al. 1981); mean plasma peaks 84.3 and 162.2 ng/ml at 9 minutes after cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992). Oral THC: bioavailability 10% to 20% with peaks at about 4 to 6 hours (Wall et al. 1983) or about 6% with peaks of 4.4 to 11 ng/ml at 1 to 5 hours (Ohlsson et al. 1980); the author's summary is 4% to 20%. Volume of distribution about 10 l/kg (Hunt & Jones 1980; Kelly & Jones 1992) or 3.4 l/kg at steady state (Grotenhermen 2003). Terminal plasma half-life of THC about 4.1 days with frequent use (Johansson et al. 1988); THC-COOH plasma half-life up to 12.6 days in one person (Johansson et al. 1989). Urine detection after one smoked cigarette at 15 ng/ml: mean 33.7 and 88.6 hours (Huestis, Mitchell & Cone 1995).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. Several statements rest on conference presentations (Nebro et al. 2004; Smith et al. 2005; Huestis, Dickerson & Cone 1992) or on unpublished observations from the author's laboratory, given without data (11-OH-THC excreted in the urine of people with chronic use beyond the period of effects; sweat studies under way; blockade of effects by rimonabant stated without a citation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across the cited controlled studies, smoking delivers THC within seconds, with plasma peaks around 9 minutes that fall to about 60% and 20% of peak at 15 and 30 minutes and vary greatly between people (bioavailability estimates from 2% to 56%); oral THC produces lower, later (1 to 6 hours) and more irregular peaks with low bioavailability (about 4% to 20%; 6% in the GC/MS study), relatively more 11-OH-THC and longer-lasting effects. THC is stored in fat, and its terminal elimination is slow with frequent use (THC about 4.1 days; THC-COOH up to 12.6 days in plasma). Urinary THC-COOH after one smoked cigarette is detectable at 15 ng/ml for about 1.5 to 4 days on average, while one case of heavy long-term use stayed positive for 67 days and in another cannabinoids were detectable for 93 days (cut-off not given).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review is descriptive, and its Conclusions only call for further controlled studies. Where it goes beyond its data: (1) it says the time-of-use prediction models are "an objective, validated method for assessing the contribution of cannabis to accidents" (3.1.5, 3rd paragraph), but the models estimate time since use, not impairment or causal contribution, and were developed and validated in the author's own controlled studies, with plasma THC below 2 ng/ml excluded from the original models because of residual THC with frequent use; (2) plasma THC above 2 to 3 ng/ml (1.6 ng/ml in whole blood) is linked to recent use and possible impairment, while the same section notes that plasma THC falls before effects peak and that people with frequent use carry residual THC; (3) the author labels as her own hypothesis that residual THC contributes to cognitive deficits early in abstinence (2.2, 6th paragraph), and attributes to the cited authors the postulate that residual brain THC explains lasting effects (2.2, 4th paragraph); (4) the 67-day urine case is called a single extreme case, while a 93-day case is reported later (3.2.2, 5th paragraph).

timeline.event: Ohlsson et al.: plasma THC after intravenous, smoked and oral THC (in a chocolate cookie), with oral bioavailability of about 6% by GC/MS, which the review prefers to earlier radiolabel estimates.
Wall et al.: oral THC in sesame oil with bioavailability of 10% to 20% and peaks at 4 to 6 hours (radiolabel method, which the author says overestimated THC); excretion mostly in feces.

Johansson et al.: terminal plasma half-life of THC of about 4.1 days in people with frequent use, measured with isotopically labelled THC over long sampling, against earlier estimates of 24 to 36 hours; labelled THC was detected in blood for up to 13 days after four labelled cigarettes.

Huestis, Henningfield & Cone: continuous blood sampling during smoking (peaks at 9 minutes) and the first time-of-use prediction models; Kelly & Jones: intravenous THC in people with frequent and infrequent use.
Huestis & Cone: a 50% ratio between consecutive creatinine-normalised urine samples to separate new use from residual excretion, against the 150% increase proposed by Manno et al. (1984).
Fraser & Worth (2002 to 2004): in people with heavy chronic use the 50% ratio may not separate new use from residual excretion, a qualification of the 1998 proposal.
Huestis, Barnes & Smith: extended validation of the prediction models after multiple doses and at low concentrations (717 specimens), by the group that developed them.

replication.where_it_stands: A standard background source on cannabinoid pharmacokinetics as of 2007. Its route contrasts (smoking fast and variable; oral intake slow, low and long-lasting) are the baseline that later studies of edibles and vaporizers build on, but it predates modern high-THC products, studies of vaporizers and concentrates, and controlled studies of commercial edibles; claims about current products need later primary studies, for example those held in the project as sc_spindle_2018 (smoked against vaporized cannabis) and sc_vandrey_2015 (edible labelling), which were not read for this card. Each figure should be cited from the primary study named in the key findings.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC author manuscript has no funding or acknowledgement statement. The author's affiliation is Chemistry and Drug Metabolism, Intramural Research Program, National Institute on Drug Abuse, NIH, Baltimore.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author. At least 18 of the 189 references list her as an author (editors' count), including the sources of all six figures, the prediction models (developed and validated by the same group) and the creatinine-ratio work. Figures are reprinted with permission from the Journal of Analytical Toxicology, Elsevier and a 2005 Springer handbook. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Controlled within-person pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies of current products (high-THC flower, concentrates, vaporizers and commercial edibles at labelled contents) in women and men with daily as well as occasional use, with sampling long enough to capture terminal elimination, and a systematic review of route-specific bioavailability and time to peak with explicit study selection.

domains.note: No search, sources, dates or criteria; the author chose the studies.

No formal appraisal, but methodological limits are named for several bodies of evidence (radiolabel overestimation of oral THC, short sampling that underestimates half-lives, hydrolysis methods, adsorption to oral-fluid devices).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: All six figures and most of the controlled human data on smoked and oral kinetics, urine detection, prediction models, creatinine ratios, oral fluid and hair are from the author's laboratory, including conference presentations (Nebro et al. 2004; Smith et al. 2005) and unpublished observations; the prediction models are validated by the group that developed them.

The author's hypothesis about residual THC and early-abstinence cognitive deficits is labelled as such, but some statements are made without data or citation (transdermal patches as a convenient alternative to oral dosing, their low potential for misuse, why people prefer smoking, the prediction models as an objective method for assessing the contribution of cannabis to accidents).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence across routes, products and patterns of use (oral intake, daily use, women and newer products under-represented)
domains.note: The detailed human data concentrate on single smoked doses of low-THC cigarettes in small groups whose sex is mostly not given (men where it is); the review itself notes fewer oral studies and little on frequent use; vaporizers are mentioned only in passing and concentrates not at all.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment follows the worst domains (search and selection; reliance on the author's own studies). The review is a careful, data-rich summary from a leading laboratory, but its selection is unsystematic and its numbers are second-hand. Cite it for the general route contrasts and the analytical points, with each figure traced to the primary study named in the key findings; a claim resting only on it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). It reports no health outcomes and should not support claims about impairment thresholds without primary data.

key_findings.finding: Smoked THC is absorbed rapidly, with peak concentrations slightly below those after intravenous dosing (Ohlsson et al. 1980). Bioavailability estimates range from 2% to 56% (Agurell & Leander 1971; Ohlsson et al. 1982, 1985; Agurell et al. 1986); elsewhere systemic availability is put at about 8% to 24%, depending strongly on the person's experience with smoking cannabis (Ohlsson et al. 1980; Perez-Reyes et al. 1981; Lindgren et al. 1981). The number, length and spacing of puffs, hold time and inhalation volume change exposure, and people who expected active drug changed how they smoked hashish to obtain higher plasma THC (Cami et al. 1991).
key_findings.locator: 2.1.1. Smoking, 1st paragraph; 2.4.2. Percentage of THC Excreted as Urinary THC-COOH, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the author's controlled study (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992; 6 participants (N = 6; the review does not state their sex); one cigarette of 1.75% THC, about 16 mg, or 3.55%, about 34 mg; continuous blood sampling), THC was detected in plasma from the first puff, when effects began (Huestis et al. 1992, Clin Pharmacol Ther); mean peaks were 84.3 ng/ml (range 50 to 129) and 162.2 ng/ml (76 to 267), reached at 9.0 minutes; mean concentrations were about 60% and 20% of peak 15 and 30 minutes after smoking and 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours; THC stayed detectable (limit 0.5 ng/ml) for 3 to 12 hours after the lower and 6 to 27 hours after the higher dose. Large differences between individuals remained despite computer-paced puffing.
key_findings.locator: 2.1.1. Smoking, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 legends
key_findings.note: A single small study from the author's laboratory, with cigarettes of low THC content by current standards. The lower-dose cigarette is given as about 16 mg of THC here, about 18 mg in 2.4.2 and about 15.8 mg in 3.2 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Other smoked studies: mean peak plasma THC of 94.3, 107.4 and 155.1 ng/ml after single cigarettes of 1.32%, 1.97% and 2.54% THC (Perez-Reyes et al. 1982); 45.6 to 187.8 ng/ml after a 1% cigarette (Perez-Reyes et al. 1981); 33 to 118 ng/ml 3 minutes after ad libitum smoking of a cigarette of about 2% (Ohlsson et al. 1980). In the author's studies, the person with the lowest peak plasma concentration had the greatest cardiovascular response (Huestis et al. 1992).
key_findings.locator: 2.1.1. Smoking, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oral THC is absorbed more slowly, with lower and later peaks (Law et al. 1984; Ohlsson et al. 1981). Bioavailability of THC in sesame oil was reported as 10% to 20%, with plasma peaks about 4 to 6 hours after 15 to 20 mg (Wall et al. 1983; a radiolabel method that, the author notes, overestimated THC); after 20 mg in a chocolate cookie, peaks of 4.4 to 11 ng/ml came 1 to 5 hours after ingestion and bioavailability was estimated at 6% (Ohlsson et al. 1980, GC/MS). The author summarises oral bioavailability as 4% to 20%, low because of variable absorption, degradation in the stomach and extensive first-pass metabolism to 11-OH-THC and inactive metabolites.
key_findings.locator: 2.1.2. Oral, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Doses are study conditions. The 4% to 20% range is the author's summary, not attributed to one study.

key_findings.finding: After a single 10 mg dronabinol capsule in 17 volunteers, mean peaks were THC 3.8 ng/ml (range 1.1 to 12.7), 11-OH-THC 3.4 ng/ml (1.2 to 5.6) and THC-COOH 26 ng/ml (14 to 46) at 1 to 2 hours, often with two THC peaks from enterohepatic circulation (Kim & Yoon 1996). Compared with smoking, oral THC has a delayed onset, lower peak concentrations and longer-lasting effects with a delayed return to baseline (Binitie 1975; Meier & Vonesch 1997).
key_findings.locator: 2.1.2. Oral, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 11-OH-THC, an active metabolite described as equipotent with THC, reaches about 10% of THC concentrations after smoking (Wall et al. 1983), or 6% to 10% for the first 45 minutes, with mean peaks of 6.7 and 7.5 ng/ml at 13.5 minutes (range 9.0 to 22.8) (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992). After oral intake, 11-OH-THC concentrations are similar to or higher than those of THC, and ratios of 11-OH-THC to THC above 1 within 2 hours and above 1.5 after 2 hours have been proposed as markers of oral intake (Nadulski et al. 2005).
key_findings.locator: 2.1.2. Oral, 6th paragraph; 2.3.1. Hepatic Metabolism, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; 3.1.2. Smoked Cannabis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In a study by the author's group, six volunteers took THC in hemp oil or as dronabinol with meals for five days (0.39 to 14.8 mg a day): plasma THC and 11-OH-THC were rarely detected at the two lowest doses, and peak plasma concentrations at the two highest doses were below 6.5 ng/ml THC, 5.6 ng/ml 11-OH-THC and 43.0 ng/ml THC-COOH (Goodwin et al. 2006; Gustafson et al. 2003).
key_findings.locator: 2.1.2. Oral, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: 3.1.3 gives below 24.4 ng/ml for THC-COOH, and plasma THC and 11-OH-THC negative by 16 hours rather than below 0.5 ng/ml by 25 hours, for what appears to be the same study, cited there to a 2004 conference presentation (Nebro et al.).

key_findings.finding: Distribution: THC is highly lipophilic and 95% to 99% bound to plasma lipoproteins, with a large volume of distribution (about 10 l/kg, Hunt & Jones 1980 and Kelly & Jones 1992; 3.4 l/kg at steady state, Grotenhermen 2003); it goes first to well-perfused tissues and is retained in fat with repeated dosing (fat-to-brain ratio about 21:1 after 7 days and 64:1 after 27 days of exposure, Kreuz & Axelrod 1973, species not stated in the review), and in studies with radiolabelled THC less than 1% of the dose was retained in the brain (Garrett 1978; Harvey et al. 1984; species not stated).
key_findings.locator: 2.2. Distribution, 1st and 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: During repeated oral THC every 4 hours for 10 to 12 days, tolerance developed while pharmacokinetics changed little (total clearance 605 to 977 ml/min; initial volume of distribution 2.6 to 6.4 l/kg), so the tolerance was attributed to pharmacodynamic adaptation (Hunt & Jones 1980).
key_findings.locator: 2.2. Distribution, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy and breast-feeding: THC crosses the placenta, with cord-blood concentrations three to six times lower than in maternal blood and greater transfer in early pregnancy (Blackard & Tennes 1984); in one woman, THC in breast milk was 8.4 times the plasma concentration, giving an estimated infant intake of 0.01 to 0.1 mg a day if the mother smoked one or two cannabis cigarettes a day (Perez-Reyes & Wall 1982).
key_findings.locator: 2.2. Distribution, 10th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the breast-milk figure is a single case and an estimate.

key_findings.finding: Elimination: 80% to 90% of THC is excreted within 5 days (Harvey 2001; Halldin et al. 1982), more than 65% in feces and about 20% in urine (Wall et al. 1983). Because THC returns slowly from fat and recirculates through the liver and gut, the terminal plasma half-life of THC in people with frequent use was about 4.1 days with isotopically labelled THC (called deuterium-labelled in 3.1.2 and radiolabelled in 3.1.2 and 3.1.4) and sensitive methods (Johansson et al. 1988), against estimates of 24 to 36 hours from studies with shorter sampling; a THC-COOH plasma half-life of up to 12.6 days was seen in one person with chronic use (Johansson et al. 1989), and the terminal urinary THC-COOH half-life is put at 3 to 4 days (Johansson & Halldin 1989). No pharmacokinetic differences between chronic and occasional use have been substantiated (Chiang & Rapaka 1987).
key_findings.locator: 2.4. Elimination, 1st paragraph; 2.4.1. Terminal Elimination Half-Lives of THC-COOH, 1st paragraph; 3.1.2. Smoked Cannabis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 2.4.2 gives fecal excretion as 30% to 65% citing the same source, and 2.4.1 calls the THC half-life greater than 4.1 days (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: After intravenous THC in 8 men (Kelly & Jones 1992), plasma half-lives were 116.8 minutes for THC, 5.2 days for THC-COOH and 6.8 days for its glucuronide in people with frequent use, against 93.3 minutes, 6.2 days and 3.7 days in people with infrequent use; conjugated THC-COOH was still detectable after 12 days in 75% of the frequent and 25% of the infrequent group.
key_findings.locator: 3.1.1. Intravenous THC Administration, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The same 5.2 and 6.2 day values appear in 2.4.1 without a citation, after a sentence about Johansson et al.

key_findings.finding: Plasma after smoking: THC was detectable for 3.5 to 5.5 hours after two cigarettes totalling about 10 mg THC (detection limit 0.8 ng/ml; McBurney et al. 1986) but for up to 13 days for deuterated THC in the blood of people with chronic use who smoked four cigarettes containing it (detection limit 0.02 ng/ml; Johansson et al. 1988); THC-COOH peaked at 24.5 and 54.0 ng/ml and was detected for a mean of 84 and 152 hours after the lower and higher doses (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992). In people with frequent use, plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH were 0.86, 0.46 and 45.8 ng/ml at least 12 hours after last use (Peat 1989), and residual plasma THC below 2 ng/ml about 12 hours after smoking is suggested in general for people who smoke chronically (not a measured value).
key_findings.locator: 3.1.2. Smoked Cannabis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; 3.1.4. Cannabinoid Concentrations after Frequent Use, 1st paragraph; 3.1.5. Prediction Models for Estimation of Cannabis Exposure, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood concentration and effect: plasma THC begins to fall before effects peak; peak effects came when THC and THC-COOH concentrations were equal, 30 to 45 minutes after smoking began (Huestis et al. 1992). Recent use (within 6 to 8 hours) and possible impairment have been linked to plasma THC above 2 to 3 ng/ml (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992; Mason & McBay 1985), and 1.6 ng/ml in whole blood has been suggested (Gjerde et al. 1993); whole-blood concentrations are about half those in plasma.
key_findings.locator: 3.1.5. Prediction Models for Estimation of Cannabis Exposure, 1st paragraph; 3.1. Plasma Concentrations, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Suggested values cited by the review, not validated impairment thresholds; the same paragraph notes that residual THC in people with frequent use complicates interpretation.

key_findings.finding: Time-of-use prediction: two models estimate the time since smoking from one plasma sample (model I from THC, model II from the THC-COOH to THC ratio) and predicted it within their 95% confidence interval for over 90% of specimens (Huestis, Henningfield & Cone 1992). In an extended validation (38 people, 717 specimens, cigarettes of 2.64% THC, some after two doses), 99% of combined-model predictions were within the interval, 0.9% overestimated and none underestimated, including all 77 specimens with THC of 0.5 to 2.0 ng/ml (Huestis, Barnes & Smith 2005); after oral THC (18 people, 90 specimens), models I and II were correct for 74.4% and 90.0% and the combined interval for 96.7% (Smith et al. 2005, conference presentation).
key_findings.locator: 3.1.5. Prediction Models for Estimation of Cannabis Exposure, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Developed and validated by the author's group; plasma THC below 2 ng/ml was excluded from the original models because of possible residual THC with frequent use.

key_findings.finding: Urine after one smoked cigarette (6 participants; the review says six subjects and does not state their sex; Huestis, Mitchell & Cone 1995, 1996): only about 0.5% of the THC dose appeared as urinary THC-COOH over 7 days; mean peak urine THC-COOH was 89.8 and 153.4 ng/ml at 7.7 and 13.9 hours, with twelvefold variation between people; at the 15 ng/ml confirmation cut-off, the last positive sample came a mean of 33.7 hours (range 8 to 68.5) after the 1.75% cigarette and 88.6 hours (57 to 122.3) after the 3.55% cigarette, and near the cut-off positive samples were interspersed among negative ones.
key_findings.locator: 2.4.2. Percentage of THC Excreted as Urinary THC-COOH, 1st paragraph; 3.2. Urine Concentrations, 2nd paragraph; 3.2.1. THC-COOH Detection Windows in Urine, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: With heavy long-term use, urine can stay positive for weeks: one person who had used heavily for more than 10 years was positive above 20 ng/ml by immunoassay up to 67 days after last use (Ellis et al. 1985), and another person with heavy use had detectable cannabinoids for 93 days, with an excretion half-life of 32 days (Lafolie et al. 1991). The review calls the 67-day case a single extreme case and adds that the urine of a person new to cannabis may test negative by immunoassay within a few hours of smoking one cigarette. A positive urine test shows only that exposure occurred, not when, how much, by which route, or whether the person was impaired.
key_findings.locator: 3.2. Urine Concentrations, 1st paragraph; 3.2.2. Normalization of Cannabinoid Urine Concentrations to Urine Creatinine Concentrations, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Separating new use from residual excretion: in the author's controlled data, a ratio of 50% between consecutive creatinine-normalised THC-COOH concentrations was most accurate (85.4% accuracy; sensitivity 80.1%, specificity 90.2%), while the earlier proposal of a 150% increase had sensitivity 33.4% and specificity 99.8% (Huestis & Cone 1998); the 50% ratio, derived after occasional use on a research unit, may not suit heavy chronic use (Fraser & Worth 2002 to 2004).
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2. Normalization of Cannabinoid Urine Concentrations to Urine Creatinine Concentrations, 2nd, 4th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Oral fluid: THC in oral fluid comes mainly from exposure of the oral mucosa during smoking, with little from plasma; after smoking, oral fluid was THC-positive at 0.5 ng/ml for 13 ± 3 hours (range 1 to 24), with occasional positives up to 34 hours (Niedbala et al. 2001); wide variation precludes using oral-fluid concentrations as indicators of impairment. Among 139 people suspected of drug-impaired driving, an oral-fluid cut-off of 1.2 ng/ml detected plasma THC of 0.5 ng/ml or more with sensitivity 94.7% and specificity 92.0% (Laloup et al. 2006). Collection devices opened inside a smoke-filled car were contaminated, while samples from passively exposed people collected outside the car were negative (Niedbala et al. 2005).
key_findings.locator: 3.3. Oral-Fluid Testing, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 5th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Hair: of 53 hair specimens from 38 men with documented cannabis use (Huestis et al. 2007), 19 (36%) had no detectable THC or THC-COOH; detection rates were 85% with daily and 52% with non-daily use (p < 0.05); the author calls low sensitivity the weakest aspect of hair testing for cannabis.
key_findings.locator: 3.5. Cannabinoids in Hair, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The same paragraph also says about two-thirds of people with daily use and one-third with non-daily use tested positive (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: CBD: smoked bioavailability averaged 31% in five people, with fourfold variation (Ohlsson et al. 1986); oral CBD gave low and variable plasma concentrations (Agurell et al. 1981; Nadulski et al. 2005). CBD did not significantly change the clearance or volume of distribution of THC or the elimination half-lives of its metabolites, apart from slightly slowing conversion of 11-OH-THC (Hunt et al. 1981), and its partial inhibition of THC hydroxylation was small compared with overall variability (Nadulski et al. 2005). Average contents in more than 30,000 cannabis preparations seized in the US between 1980 and 1997 were 3.1% THC and 0.3% CBD (ElSohly et al. 2000).
key_findings.locator: 2.1.7. Cannabidiol Absorption, 2nd paragraph; 2.3.3. Metabolism of Cannabidiol, 1st paragraph; 2.1.1. Smoking, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Unit errors: hemp oil is said to have had THC contents of at least 300 and 1,500 mg/g (more than the oil's own mass for the second value); urinary THC-COOH is given as 93.9 ± 24.5 mg with a range in µg; hair limits of quantification are given as 1.0 and 0.1 pg/mg and, in the same paragraph, as 1 and 0.1 ng/mg; a pig study is described as giving 200 mg/kg intravenously (not checked against the primary, Brunet et al. 2006).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 2.1.2. Oral, 4th paragraph; 2.4.2, 1st paragraph; 3.5, 4th paragraph; 2.2. Distribution, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these values can be quoted without checking the primary source; the hemp-oil figures are probably µg/g.

reporting_issues.issue: The THC content of the lower-dose cigarette in the author's smoking studies is given as about 16 mg (2.1.1), about 18 mg (2.4.2) and about 15.8 mg (3.2); the urinary recoveries of 0.54% and 0.53% cannot be reproduced exactly from the printed means (93.9 µg of 18 mg is 0.52% and of 15.8 mg 0.59%; 197.4 µg of 34 mg is 0.58%; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 2.1.1, 2nd paragraph; 2.4.2, 1st paragraph; 3.2, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; describe the cigarettes by THC percentage, and the recovery as about 0.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: Fecal excretion is given as more than 65% (2.4) and as 30% to 65% (2.4.2), both citing Wall et al. (1983); the terminal plasma half-life of THC is greater than 4.1 days in 2.4.1 but about 4.1 days in 3.1.2 and 3.1.4.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 2.4, 1st paragraph; 2.4.1, 1st paragraph; 2.4.2, 1st paragraph; 3.1.2, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote the fecal share as most of the dose, and the half-life as about 4 days with frequent use, citing Johansson et al. (1988).

reporting_issues.issue: For what appears to be the same hemp-oil and dronabinol study, 2.1.2 gives peak THC-COOH below 43.0 ng/ml and THC and 11-OH-THC below 0.5 ng/ml by 25 hours (citing Goodwin et al. 2006 and Gustafson et al. 2003), while 3.1.3 gives below 24.4 ng/ml and negative by 16 hours (citing a 2004 conference presentation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the peer-reviewed sources' figures and check them in the primaries.

reporting_issues.issue: In the hair study, detection rates are given as 85% (daily use) and 52% (non-daily use), and later in the same paragraph as about two-thirds and one-third.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 3.5. Cannabinoids in Hair, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The detection rates must be taken from the primary study (Huestis et al. 2007) before citing.

reporting_issues.issue: In 2.4.1, mean plasma THC-COOH half-lives of 5.2 ± 0.8 and 6.2 ± 6.7 days for frequent and infrequent use follow a sentence about Johansson et al. (1989) without a citation; the same values are attributed to Kelly & Jones (1992) in 3.1.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Attribute these half-lives to Kelly & Jones (1992).

reporting_issues.issue: The smoked bioavailability of CBD is printed as 31 13% in five subjects, with a symbol missing (probably 31 ± 13%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 2.1.7. Cannabidiol Absorption, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote only the mean (31%) and the fourfold variation.

reporting_issues.issue: Adams & Martin are said to have calculated that 2 to 22 mg of THC in a cigarette delivers 0.2 to 4.4 mg, based on a bioavailability of 10% to 25%; 22 mg at 25% would be 5.5 mg, so the upper figure corresponds to 20% (editors' calculation).

After reporting that THC-COOH was found in 76.2% of oral-fluid specimens, the review says this suggests a definitive means of distinguishing passive exposure from use, and then calls it a limitation that has curtailed oral-fluid testing; the two sentences contradict each other.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 3.3. Oral-Fluid Testing, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The passage cannot be cited for either reading.

reporting_issues.issue: The creatinine-ratio data set is described as more than 1,800 pairs of urine specimens in one paragraph and as more than 1,800 specimens in another; elsewhere no significant differences are reported with P ≤ 0.05.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 3.2.2, 4th and 6th paragraphs; 2.4.2, 3rd paragraph
